questions.q: Prior $\text{Beta}(2, 2)$ on a coin's heads probability $p$. You observe 7 heads and 3 tails. What is the posterior and its mean?
questions.explain: Conjugacy just adds counts: $\text{Beta}(\alpha+h, \beta+t) = \text{Beta}(9, 5)$ with mean $9/14 \approx 0.643$. That lies between the prior mean $0.5$ and the MLE $h/n = 0.7$ — the prior acts like 4 extra pseudo-flips.

options: U-shaped: density shoots up near both $p = 0$ and $p = 1$
Decreasing, with all its mass near $p = 0$
questions.explain: With $\alpha, \beta < 1$ the factors $p^{\alpha-1}$ and $(1-p)^{\beta-1}$ blow up at both edges, so the density is U-shaped. Its mean is still $0.5$, but $0.5$ is the *least* likely region. Flat is $\text{Beta}(1, 1)$.

questions.q: An ad got 0 clicks in 8 views. Using Laplace smoothing (posterior mean under a $\text{Beta}(1, 1)$ prior), what is the estimated click-through rate?
questions.explain: Posterior $\text{Beta}(1+0, 1+8)$ has mean $(h+1)/(n+2) = 1/10$. The MLE would be $0/8 = 0$, which wrongly claims the ad can never be clicked.

questions.q: In Thompson sampling, why does an arm that has been pulled only a few times still get played sometimes?
options: A fixed fraction of rounds is reserved for random exploration
Its wide posterior occasionally produces the largest sampled $\theta$, so it is chosen in proportion to the chance it is the best arm
The algorithm always plays the arm with the fewest pulls
It only happens until the first win, then the arm is dropped
questions.explain: Each round draws one $\theta_i$ from every arm's Beta posterior and plays the argmax. Uncertain arms have spread-out posteriors, so they sometimes win the draw; as evidence accumulates their posteriors concentrate and bad arms are played less. There is no fixed $\varepsilon$ (that is $\varepsilon$-greedy).
